newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Amnesty assails China's plan to curb HK liberties.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty assails China's plan to curb HK liberties.

text.p: The Amnesty International human rights organisation assailed China's plan to amend Hong Kong laws on Friday, saying the move could severely damage human rights guarantees that had helped make the territory so dynamic.
The laws that face the axe when Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 include parts of the Bill of Rights and legislation allowing freedom of assembly and association.
If the amendments are adopted, post-handover authorities would have greater leeway to ban protests seen as critical of China or the new Hong Kong government, Amnesty said.
The authorities would also find it easier to close down non-governmental organisations (NGOs), the London-based group said in a faxed statement to media. Amnesty itself is an NGO.

"Hong Kong has a thriving community of NGOs and human rights activists," Amnesty said. "NGOs make an important contribution to Hong Kong's open and dynamic society. They should not be intimidated by the threat of a ban."
Amnesty appealed to Tung Chee-hwa, who was chosen to be Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader by a Beijing-backed committee, to ensure laws that protect human rights were kept intact.

"Chief Executive-Designate Tung Chee-hwa has said he will work for the interests of all Hong Kong's people. The best way to show this would be to commit himself to ensuring that all existing safeguards for human rights are maintained," it said.
Tung has defended the changes proposed by a Beijing-controlled panel, saying they were necessary to strike "the right balance between individual rights and social order".

Pro-democracy activists staged a small but noisy protest on Friday morning at Tung's office, the first in a series of planned protest actions. Hong Kong has been a British colony for more than 150 years.
